turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I daresay you are aware, Mr. Worthing, that a house in Belgrave Square is not exactly the kind of establishment one would wish to associate with one's daughter, especially at her tender age.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I have no idea what you're trying to imply, mamma, but I assure you, my engagement to Jack is perfectly respectable.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that I am not altogether pleased with the manner in which you have thus far presented yourself.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I'm surprised you're questioning Jack's character, mamma, when I'm the one who's been engaged to him all along.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't quite understand what you're suggesting, Lady Bracknell. I thought I'd made it quite clear that I'm a respectable young man, despite my humble circumstances.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist, Mr. Worthing, that you provide me with a satisfactory explanation for your rather...unconventional name, and the lack of any reputable references to support your claims of respectability.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I must say, mamma, that I'm growing quite tired of these baseless accusations. Can't you see that Jack is a perfectly respectable young man, and that I'm the one who knows him best?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, I am not at all convinced by your protestations of respectability, Mr. Worthing. Your dubious surname and the lack of any reputable connections to your family are most...disturbing.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mamma, I've told you before - my name is Worthing, and I've explained the circumstances surrounding it. Can't you accept that?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist on seeing some proof of your family connections, Mr. Worthing. A respectable young man such as yourself should be able to produce some respectable relatives to vouch for him.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't have any living relatives who could vouch for me, Lady Bracknell. I'm rather an only child, and my parents passed away when I was quite young.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: This is a very serious matter, Mr. Worthing. I must insist that you provide me with the names of your guardians, or those who brought you up, so that I may be able to verify your respectable upbringing.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mamma, stop being so absurd! I'm not going to let you scare Jack off with your ridiculous questions.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am not being absurd, Gwendolen. I am merely ensuring that you do not marry a young man without a suitable pedigree. Now, Mr. Worthing, I must insist on knowing the names of your guardians, if you have any.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't have any names to give you, Lady Bracknell. I was brought up by my uncle, but he's dead now too.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I dare say, Mr. Worthing, you are not making a very satisfactory impression so far. Tell me, how is it that you came to be known as Jack Worthing, if you have no living relatives to vouch for you?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid it's a bit of a long story, Lady Bracknell, but I was brought up by my father, and he's the one who gave me the name. He was a kind man, and I'm rather proud of my family, even if it's not, uh, terribly aristocratic.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, your family history is rather...fascinating. Tell me, what is the nature of your father's relationship to you, if you may say so yourself?

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mamma, please don't be so ridiculous. Jack's family is perfectly respectable, and I'm not going to let you drive a wedge between us.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist, Mr. Worthing, on a full and satisfactory explanation of your parentage, and I warn you that I shall not be satisfied with any vague or evasive replies.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
